To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a monocentric land-use pattern exists when the population density is low, (2) a completely integrated land-use pattern exists in a large city, (3) a partially integrated (with central integration) pattern exists when the city is not too small, and (4) a partially integrated pattern (with urban fringe integration) exists when the city has a large population and the population density is not too high.
the port-city model generates the four different land-use patterns depending on parameter values.

the port city can generate four types of urban land-use patterns, namely, (i) monocentric, with the port at the city center, (ii) integrated, with the port integrated with the rest of the city, (iii) partially integrated, with the integration at the center, and (iv) partially integrated, but with the integration at urban fringe, and that the last pattern suggests the explanation of the suburbanization of employment in the city.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following three points: (1) the general equilibrium analysis of the urban spatial structure; (2) the port-city model; and (3) the suburbanization of employment.

the Cobb-Douglas model of a port city can generate a variety of spatial structures, and it is the port-city model itself that is responsible for the variety of spatial structures.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the general equilibrium approach is a powerful tool for the study of urban spatial structure.
the port-city model can generate all possible land-use patterns, but the port-city model is a special case of the general equilibrium urban spatial model.
the port‐city model is capable of generating a wide variety of land-use patterns.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the port-city model, when appropriately specified, can explain the suburbanization of employment in the presence of a port city.
the spatial structure of a city is determined by the relative sizes of the city's port and nonport activities and the relative sizes of port and nonport land-use activities.

, if we take into account the spatial structure of production activities and their interdependence with consumption activities in a general equilibrium framework, we can explain the observed spatial structures of cities in a much more comprehensive way than in the previous models.
